title: Dermoid & Epidermoid Cysts: Ophthalmic Insights
summary: Dermoid and epidermoid cysts are common congenital choristomas in the periorbital and orbital regions, originating from sequestered ectodermal tissues. While typically benign, their diverse presentations, potential for deep orbital or intracranial extension, and risk of inflammatory rupture necessitate precise diagnosis and meticulous surgical management to prevent complications and recurrence.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content:
**Dermoid Cysts**: Congenital choristomatous lesions resulting from sequestration of ectodermal tissues (epidermis, dermis, and adnexal structures like hair follicles, sebaceous and sweat glands) at sites of embryonic fusion lines. They are typically benign, slow-growing, and present as soft, non-tender masses, often in the periorbital region.

**Epidermoid Cysts**: Also congenital choristomas, formed by sequestration of only epidermal elements (keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium) without dermal adnexal structures. They are filled with desquamated keratin, giving them a pearly appearance. Epidermoids tend to grow slower than dermoids but can rupture and cause significant inflammatory reactions.

content.description: Orbital dermoid cysts are the most common congenital orbital masses (3-9% of all orbital tumors, up to 50% of pediatric orbital lesions). More common in children and young adults, typically unilateral.

branches: Entrapment of full-thickness surface ectoderm (epidermis + dermis + adnexa)
Growth: Sebaceous gland activity contributes to slower growth than epidermoids, but contents accumulation leads to gradual enlargement.
Growth: Slow accumulation of keratin, often pearly appearance. Less prone to rupture than dermoids but spillage causes severe inflammation.

rows: **By Location**
Superficial / Periorbital
Most common (lateral brow, superonasal, eyelid). Present early, often palpable.
Deep Orbital
Within muscle cone, lacrimal fossa, retrobulbar. Can cause proptosis, globe displacement. May present later.
Intracranial / Intracranial Extension
From orbit or isolated. Can cause neurological symptoms. Requires neurosurgical evaluation.
Conjunctival / Epibulbar
Rare. Small, firm nodule on bulbar conjunctiva, often limbal.
**By Histology**
Dermoid Cyst
Lined by stratified squamous epithelium with dermal adnexal structures (hair follicles, sebaceous/sweat glands) in the wall.
Epidermoid Cyst
Lined by stratified squamous epithelium WITHOUT dermal adnexal structures. Contents purely keratin.

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: **General**: Slow-growing, non-tender, firm, palpable mass. Often noticed in childhood.

**Superficial Dermoids**: Well-demarcated, rubbery, mobile (unless tethered to periosteum), non-transilluminable. Located at bony sutures (e.g., lateral aspect of superior orbital rim, medial canthus). Overlying skin usually normal.

**Deep Orbital Dermoids**: Proptosis (axial or non-axial), globe displacement (e.g., inferonasal with superior-temporal lesion), diplopia, pain (if inflamed or large). Rare compressive optic neuropathy leading to vision loss.

**Ruptured Cyst**: Acute onset of inflammation, pain, erythema, and swelling ('chemical cellulitis') due to spillage of sebaceous or keratinous contents. Can mimic acute infection or orbital cellulitis.
**Intracranial Extension**: Headaches, seizures, cranial nerve palsies, focal neurological deficits (rare, but serious).

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings
content: **Inspection & Palpation**: Well-demarcated, firm-to-rubbery, non-compressible, non-pulsatile, non-tender mass. May be fixed to periosteum (especially superficial lesions) or mobile. Proptosis, globe displacement, or eyelid malposition.
**Slit-lamp**: For conjunctival lesions, a pearly white subconjunctival nodule, often at the limbus. May cause astigmatism if large.
**Motility**: Restricted eye movements in fields of gaze if a deep orbital mass impinges on extraocular muscles.
**Fundoscopy**: Typically normal. Rarely, choroidal folds or optic disc edema with large retrobulbar lesions causing increased orbital pressure or direct optic nerve compression.
**Vision**: Usually normal unless optic nerve compression or significant globe distortion leading to astigmatism or refractive error changes.

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **Step 1: Clinical Assessment** - Detailed history (onset, duration, growth, symptoms), comprehensive ophthalmic examination including palpation of orbital rims and assessment of proptosis/globe displacement.
**Step 2: Imaging (Crucial)**

**Computed Tomography (CT) Scan**: Ideal for bony architecture. Reveals a well-circumscribed, hypodense orbital mass (fat density for dermoids, similar to CSF for epidermoids). Bone remodeling/scalloping of adjacent bone is common. Identifies calcification (rare) and bony erosion/intracranial extension.
**Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)**: Superior for soft tissue characterization and delineating intracranial extension.
*   **Dermoid**: Hyperintense on T1-weighted images (due to fat), variable signal on T2. Fat suppression sequences (STIR/FLAIR) show signal drop-out. Typically no post-contrast enhancement.
*   **Epidermoid**: Hypo- to isointense on T1, hyperintense on T2 (similar to CSF but with restricted diffusion on DWI). No enhancement. 'Pearly' appearance due to keratin.
**Step 3: Biopsy (Rarely primary)** - Only considered if imaging is inconclusive or malignancy is strongly suspected. Goal is usually complete excisional biopsy.

rows: **Encephalocele/Meningocele**
Soft, pulsatile, reducible mass; may transilluminate; positive Valsalva maneuver.
Direct intracranial communication (confirmed by imaging), pulsatility, reducibility, absence of fat/keratin on MRI.
**Capillary Hemangioma**
Bluish discoloration, increases in size with crying/straining; early onset in infancy.
Blanching with pressure, characteristic rapid growth then involution, vascular flow voids/enhancement on imaging.
**Lymphangioma/Venous Malformation**
Diffuse, spongy, ill-defined mass; can have sudden enlargement from hemorrhage.
Lack of well-defined capsule, presence of fluid levels (blood) on imaging, no bony remodeling.
**Rhabdomyosarcoma**
Rapidly progressive proptosis, typically in young children, highly aggressive, destructive bone changes.
Rapid growth, infiltrative margins, aggressive bone destruction, highly malignant histological features.
**Orbital Cellulitis**
Acute onset, pain, erythema, fever, restricted motility, systemic signs of infection.
Warm, tender, diffuse inflammatory changes on imaging, history of recent infection (e.g., sinusitis).
**Mucocele**
Originates from frontal/ethmoid sinus expansion, proptosis, globe displacement.
Clear connection to paranasal sinus, thin-walled cyst filled with mucus, distinct imaging appearance of sinus involvement.
**Lacrimal Gland Lesions**
Superotemporal orbital mass, inferonasal globe displacement.
Location within lacrimal fossa, specific imaging characteristics of lacrimal gland tumors (e.g., pleomorphic adenoma).
**Neurofibroma (Plexiform)**
S-shaped eyelid deformity, diffuse involvement, associated with NF1.
Infiltrative nature, 'bag of worms' palpation, associated systemic findings of Neurofibromatosis Type 1.

sections.title: 9. Staging / Grading
content: There is no formal 'staging' system (like TNM) for dermoid/epidermoid cysts.
However, their location and characteristics are crucial for prognosis and surgical planning:
**Superficial Lesions**: Generally excellent prognosis with complete excision. Low surgical morbidity.
**Deep Orbital Lesions**: Higher surgical complexity, increased risk of proptosis, compressive neuropathy, and potential for incomplete excision if challenging location.
**Intracranial Extension**: Significant surgical risk, requires multidisciplinary approach (neurosurgery). Potential for CSF leak, neurological sequelae.

**Cyst Rupture**: Induces a severe granulomatous inflammatory reaction, making dissection extremely difficult, increasing risk of incomplete removal and recurrence. This is a critical prognostic factor.

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment Algorithm
content: **Step 1: Diagnosis & Assessment**
Confirm diagnosis with thorough history, examination, and essential imaging (CT/MRI).
Evaluate size, location, relationship to vital structures, and rule out intracranial extension.
**Step 2: Decision for Surgical Excision**
**Indications**: Cosmetic deformity, symptomatic (proptosis, diplopia, pain, vision changes), risk of rupture (especially large cysts), uncertainty in diagnosis (rarely).

**Timing**: Generally elective. For superficial lesions, may be deferred for cosmetic reasons in older children. Urgent if vision-threatening or acute rupture/inflammation (may delay if inflammation is severe, treat with steroids first).
**Step 3: Pre-operative Planning**
Detailed review of imaging with surgeon. Discuss potential surgical approaches.
If intracranial extension, multidisciplinary consultation with neurosurgery.
**Step 4: Surgical Excision**
**Goal**: Complete, intact removal of the cyst to prevent recurrence and inflammatory reaction from spillage of contents.
**Technique**: Meticulous, blunt dissection along the capsule. Use appropriate orbitotomy approach (see section 11).
**Step 5: Post-operative Care**
Routine orbital surgery care. Monitor for complications (hematoma, infection, recurrence, CSF leak).
Histopathological confirmation of diagnosis.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques: Approach by Location
content: **General Principle**: Meticulous blunt dissection to preserve the cyst capsule intact and avoid spillage, which can cause severe inflammation and recurrence.
**Superficial Periorbital (Lateral Brow, Medial Canthus)**:
**Incision**: Skin incision directly over the mass (for easy access) or hidden within a natural skin crease (e.g., eyebrow, upper eyelid crease, subciliary) for cosmetic results.
**Approach**: Dissect down to the fibrous capsule. Bluntly separate from surrounding tissues, often adherent to periosteum at a bony suture. Remove intact.
**Deep Orbital (Intraconal / Extraconal)**:
**Anterior Orbitotomy**: For lesions anterior to the orbital equator (e.g., through eyelid crease, subciliary, or transconjunctival approaches).
**Lateral Orbitotomy (Kronlein-Berke)**: For lesions in the lateral or posterior orbit. Involves detachment of temporalis muscle and temporary removal of a bone flap.
**Medial Orbitotomy**: For lesions near the medial wall/apex, sometimes combined with ethmoidectomy or transcaruncular approach (avoids visible skin incision).
**Intracranial Extension**: Requires combined craniotomy with neurosurgical collaboration for safe dissection and closure of dural defects.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Intraoperative Complications**:
**Cyst Rupture**: Most common. Leads to severe granulomatous inflammation ('chemical cellulitis'), making further dissection difficult, increasing recurrence risk.
Hemorrhage, damage to extraocular muscles, optic nerve, lacrimal gland, globe perforation (rare).
CSF leak (if intracranial communication or inadvertent dural tear).
**Postoperative Complications**:
Infection, hematoma, lid malposition (ptosis, lagophthalmos), diplopia, globe dystopia, persistent inflammation (from rupture), residual cyst/recurrence (if incomplete excision).
Vision loss (rare, but possible with optic nerve injury or severe orbital compartment syndrome).

**Prognosis**: Excellent with complete, intact surgical excision. Recurrence rate is low (1-2%) if removed entirely. If the cyst ruptures during surgery, the risk of recurrence increases significantly (up to 20-30%) due to residual epithelial cells and chronic inflammation.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **Rapidly Enlarging Orbital Mass**: Suggests aggressive tumor or acute inflammation/hemorrhage.
**Acute Onset of Pain, Erythema, and Swelling**: Especially with an existing mass, highly suggestive of cyst rupture and severe inflammation, mimicking orbital cellulitis.
**Progressive Proptosis or Globe Displacement**: Indicates increasing orbital mass effect, potentially compressing vital structures.
**New or Worsening Diplopia**: Suggests impingement on extraocular muscles or nerves.
**Decreased Visual Acuity or Afferent Pupillary Defect**: Sign of optic nerve compression, requiring urgent evaluation.
**Signs of Intracranial Involvement**: Headache, neurological changes (e.g., seizures, cranial nerve palsies), or meningeal signs; indicates urgent neurosurgical consultation.
**Any Suspicion of Malignancy**: Rapid growth, destructive features on imaging, or atypical presentation should prompt urgent workup.

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Dermoid cysts are **choristomas** (normal tissue in an abnormal location), while epidermoids are a simpler form with only epidermal elements.
**Imaging (CT/MRI)** is paramount for diagnosis, surgical planning, and ruling out intracranial extension.
Always suspect a dermoid cyst when encountering a mass at **bony suture lines** (e.g., lateral brow, medial canthus) in children.
A **ruptured dermoid cyst** causes a severe granulomatous inflammatory reaction, mimicking infection. Corticosteroids may be used to reduce inflammation pre-operatively if ruptured.
**Incomplete excision**, especially after rupture, is the primary cause of recurrence.
Epidermoid cysts can be distinguished on MRI by **diffusion restriction** (high signal on DWI/low ADC) due to their keratin content, similar to epidermoid cholesteatomas elsewhere.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content:
Recent advancements focus on enhancing diagnostic precision and minimizing surgical morbidity.

*   **Advanced Imaging**: Continuous improvement in MRI sequences, including advanced fat suppression and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), provides better tissue characterization and delineation of cyst contents (fat vs. keratin) and anatomical relationships, aiding in surgical planning for complex cases, especially deep orbital or intracranial lesions.
*   **Minimally Invasive Surgery**: Increased adoption of endoscopic and transcaruncular approaches for select superficial and medial orbital dermoids, aiming for reduced scarring, faster recovery, and improved cosmetic outcomes, particularly in pediatric patients. Robotic assistance in orbital surgery is an evolving area.
*   **Pathophysiology of Rupture**: Better understanding of the inflammatory cascade induced by cyst rupture (e.g., foreign body giant cell reaction) has led to more refined management strategies, often involving pre-operative corticosteroids to calm acute inflammation, making subsequent surgical dissection safer and potentially reducing recurrence.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Pediatric Prevalence**: Dermoid cysts are the most common orbital mass in children, often noticed at birth or in early infancy. Growth may be slow, but they can cause cosmetic deformity or mass effect over time.

**Surgical Timing**: Generally elective. For superficial lesions, surgery can be deferred to later childhood for better patient cooperation and a larger surgical field, unless rapidly growing, symptomatic, or cosmetically distressing. Deep or symptomatic lesions may warrant earlier intervention.
**Anesthesia**: General anesthesia is required for all pediatric patients.

**Careful Dissection**: Especially crucial in children to avoid damaging developing orbital structures and to ensure complete removal without rupture, as recurrence can be more complex and distressing in this population. Long-term follow-up is important.
